title: Midsummer in Vell

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Twenty-Fourth Saying: Show your work. A truth that cannot be checked is only an opinion with good posture.*

The Great Hall of the Meridian Guild smelled of beeswax, polished brass, and the specific, nervous scent of people who had dressed for an occasion they did not understand. It was Midsummer morning, and the light fell in long, golden shafts through the high clerestory windows, illuminating dust motes that danced in the stale air like tiny, suspended stars. The floor was a vast expanse of grey marble veined with black, reflecting the assembled crowd. The Guild Masters wore their grey coats, while the nobles rustled in silks that spoke of expensive authority. In a corner slightly apart stood the farmers from the Marches in their Sunday best, looking as though they had wandered into a library and expected to find a loaf of bread.

Isla stood at the head of a long, high table. She wore her mustard-yellow canvas surveyor's coat, the pockets bulging with the debris of forty days in the Unmade: a snapped lead pencil, a coil of twine, and a small, cold stone from the Salt Flat. Her hair was twisted high, the two crossed brass pencils holding it in place, though one was slightly askew. Beside her, Master Vasht leaned on his carved walking stick, his grey wool coat rumpled, his expression one of profound, dignified patience. To her other side stood Joss, his sleeves rolled up, a carpenter's pencil behind his ear, and Mags, her blue scarf tied tightly, her iron cooking pot secured to her back. Behind them, Sera Quillon stood with her hands clasped, her plum-purple velvet coat crisp, her face a mask of professional neutrality that Isla recognized as a very thin veil of anxiety.

On the table before them lay two sheets of guild paper. One was the Chancellor’s fast sheet, a masterpiece of elegant, sweeping lines that promised order and profit. The other was Isla’s survey, a dense, intricate web of triangles, contours, and notes, a document that showed its work as clearly as a mathematician shows a proof.

The Royal Surveyor, a man with a face like a cracked walnut, stood at the end of the table, his level and staff ready. He adjusted his spectacles, looked at the two sheets, and then at Isla, with an expression that suggested he was deciding whether to sigh or to faint.

"Your Majesty," the Guild Master began, his voice echoing in the vaulted space, "we are ready to adjudicate the survey of the Unmade."

The Queen, Queen Cassia of Aster, sat on a simple chair at the center of the room, her plain silver circlet catching the light. She did not look at the Guild Master. She looked at Isla.

"Begin," she said.
pages.image: In a grand marble hall with high arched windows, Isla in a mustard coat and brass pencils in her hair stands beside a long table holding two large map sheets, flanked by an older man in a grey coat leaning on a stick, a freckled young man in a red shirt, and a girl in a teal jacket, while a Queen in a blue gown watches from a simple chair.

pages.text:
Lord Chancellor Aldous Vane stepped forward. He was a tall man, his pearl-grey frock coat immaculate, his silver hair swept back from a face that smiled with the ease of a man who had never once been told "no." He gestured gracefully toward his sheet, and the hall leaned in, drawn by the sheer polish of his presentation.

"This," Vane said, his voice smooth as poured cream, "is the future of the Marches. We speak of a reservoir that will irrigate three counties, turning the dry scrub into grain estates of unprecedented yield. We speak of a grand road, straight and true, cutting through the wilderness to bring the bounty of the Unmade to the markets of Vell. It is efficient. It is profitable. And, above all, it is done."

He tapped the sheet with his gold-topped cane. "The land is a resource to be managed, not a mystery to be solved. This sheet offers certainty. It offers growth."

Murmurs rippled through the crowd. The farmers shifted, some nodding, others frowning. Isla felt a cold weight settle in her stomach, not of fear, but of the specific, heavy dread of watching someone lie beautifully.

Vane turned his gaze to Isla. His smile did not waver, but his eyes were sharp, assessing.

"And this?" he asked, nodding at Isla’s sheet. "What do we have here, Miss Corrin? A charming hobby of unregistered apprentices? A drawing of hills that wandered off during the tea break? It is cluttered. It is indecisive. It is, in the language of the Guild, a failure to deliver."

He spread his hands, a gesture of dismissive pity. "You have spent forty days in the mud, measuring stones that move. I have spent forty days ensuring that the kingdom eats. I trust Your Majesty will not punish efficiency for the sake of sentiment."

Isla looked at Joss. He gave a small, almost imperceptible nod. *Show your work,* his eyes seemed to say.

She stepped forward, her boots clicking on the marble. The sound was small, but in the sudden silence, it rang like a bell.

"Your Majesty," Isla said, her voice steady, "I would like to answer."
pages.image: In the grand hall, a tall man in a pearl-grey coat and gold cane gestures elegantly at a map sheet on a table, smiling confidently, while in the foreground a girl in a mustard coat stands with her chin up, her expression serious and resolute, the Queen in blue watching intently from her chair.

pages.text:
Isla did not speak immediately. Instead, she reached into the deep pocket of her mustard-yellow coat and withdrew a small, leather-bound book. Its spine was cracked, the pages soft with the friction of years and repeated use. She placed it on the marble table, right beside her own sheet, with the precise care one shows when setting down a fragile instrument.

"This," she said, her voice level and clear, "is the field-book of Hester Corrin, my great-grandmother. She surveyed Ennis Vale forty-four years ago. Her work was condemned for a closing error. The valley was declared loose, and it was lost from the Atlas."

She pulled out a second book, thicker and bound in grey cloth. "This is the Guild’s own record of the benchmark in Vell. The brass disc set in the floor of the Atlas Room. It is the point from which the entire city is measured."

With a final motion, she placed her own field-book down. It lay open to the pages where the transposed digit had been corrected, the error owned, and the truth restored. The ink was dry, the columns neat, the calculations redundant and checked.

"I am not asking Your Majesty to believe me," Isla said. The silence in the hall was thick, but her voice carried through it without strain. "I am not asking you to trust my word, or my family’s name, or the eloquence of the Lord Chancellor. I am asking you to check it. Because a truth that cannot be checked is only an opinion with good posture."

She looked up at the Queen, holding her gaze steady. "I have shown my work. Every angle, every level, every correction is written down. The numbers are there. If I am wrong, let the numbers say so. If the Chancellor is right, let his sheet stand. But let us find out which one is true."

The Queen’s eyes narrowed slightly. She looked at Vane, who had the grace to look slightly uncomfortable, shifting his weight from one foot to the other. She then turned to the Royal Surveyor, standing rigid by the wall.

"Set up the level," she said. "Read the known points. And compare the two sheets."

The Royal Surveyor bowed, a jerky, uncertain motion. He picked up his instrument, his face pale as paper. He looked at the two sheets, then at the Queen, and then at Isla, who met his gaze with a calm, steady eye. There was no hesitation in her posture, only the quiet confidence of a hand that has held a line true.

"Very well, Your Majesty," he said. "We shall see."
pages.image: On the marble floor of the hall, a man in a dark coat sets up a brass surveying level on a tripod, adjusting it carefully, while Isla, exactly one Isla stands nearby with her hands clasped, watching intently, the Queen in blue observing from the side.

pages.text:
The Royal Surveyor moved with the meticulous caution of a man attempting to repair a cracked lens rather than a broken reputation. He unfolded the tripod legs, screwed them into the marble floor until they bit, and leveled the bubble until it sat centered in its circle, a small, perfect eye. He raised the staff to the first point, the brass benchmark disc embedded in the floor, and read the number. Then he turned the instrument to the second point, a stone pillar near the heavy oak doors, and read that number too.

He turned to the two sheets laid out on the table. On Vane’s sheet, the distance between these two points was marked by a single, confident line, drawn with the easy assurance of a man who had never once had to check his work. On Isla’s sheet, the same distance was embedded in a complex triangle, surrounded by angles, checks, and a small, neat column of calculations in the margin.

The Surveyor did the arithmetic. He checked it. He checked it again, his finger tracing the numbers with the same slow, deliberate rhythm he used when tying a knot in rope.

"There is a discrepancy," he said, his voice tight and thin as wire. "On the Chancellor’s sheet, the distance is off. By thirty feet. On the apprentice’s sheet, it is within the width of a thumb."

Murmurs rippled through the hall, soft at first, then rising like wind in a rigging. The farmers leaned forward, their elbows on the table. The nobles exchanged glances that held no warmth. Vane’s smile faltered, just for a moment, a hairline crack in the porcelain of his composure.

"Impossible," Vane said, the smoothness draining from his voice. "There must be an error in your reading."

"My reading is not the issue," the Surveyor said, his eyes fixed on the Queen, refusing to look at the Chancellor. "The error is in the benchmark. The Chancellor’s sheet was measured from a point that does not match the Guild’s official record. It is a rigged point. A false anchor."

The Queen’s face was unreadable, her silver circlet catching the light from the high windows. She looked at Vane, who had gone very still, his gold-topped cane gripped so tightly his knuckles had whitened.

"Lord Chancellor," she said, her voice quiet and precise, "you mentioned the financing of the dam. You said it was a matter of efficiency. But if the benchmark is false, then the entire survey is built on a lie. And a lie, no matter how beautiful, does not hold the land."

Vane’s mouth opened, then closed. He said nothing. The silence in the room was not empty; it was full, heavy, and waiting.

Isla felt a surge of something that was not triumph, but a deep, quiet relief, the kind that settles in the chest after a long climb. The land had been measured. The truth had been checked. And the numbers, for once, had spoken without needing to shout.
pages.image: In the hall, a man in a dark coat points to a map sheet, his expression serious, while a tall man in a pearl-grey coat stands with his face pale and rigid, Isla, exactly one Isla watching with a calm, satisfied expression, the Queen in blue looking sternly at the man in grey.

pages.text:
Master Vasht stepped forward. The room hushed, not with the sudden stop of a struck bell, but with the held breath of a man waiting for a reading to settle. His voice was soft, yet it carried, cutting through the stillness with the quiet, undeniable precision of a compass needle finding north.

"Your Majesty," he said, "I must speak. Forty-four years ago, I was a junior clerk at this Guild. I reported the survey of Hester Corrin as faulty. I followed the Guild’s finding. I did not check the benchmark. I did not question the numbers. I was wrong. And my haste has cost this kingdom a valley."

He turned his gaze to Isla. His eyes were bright, carrying a grief that had been packed away in the corners of his memory for decades, only now to be unpacked in the open light. "I am sorry. I am sorry to her. I am sorry to you."

The silence in the hall was absolute. The Guild Master, a man whose face had turned the pale grey of old parchment, rose to his feet with a slow, deliberate motion.

"The Guild," he said, his voice trembling slightly, "will reopen the sheet. We will review the benchmark. We will correct the record."

A low hum moved through the crowd, a resonant sound of recognition and regret that seemed to vibrate in the floorboards. Isla looked down at her hands. She realized she had been gripping Joss’s hand so tightly that the skin of his knuckles had gone white beneath her fingers. He had not let go. He had not said a single word. He had just been there, steady and sure, acting as a counterweight to her own trembling, anchoring her to the ground as if he were a fixed point on a map.

She squeezed his hand, just once. It was a small, silent acknowledgment, a promise made without the need for any further explanation.

The Queen stood, her silver circlet catching the light from the high windows. She looked at Isla, then at Vane, and finally at the two sheets laid out on the table.

"Take the Chancellor’s sheet down," she said. "And bring me the field-books. I want to see the work."

Isla felt the responsibility of the moment settle onto her shoulders. It was not a burden, but a duty, clear and sharp-edged like a well-honed chisel. She had measured the land. She had shown her work. And now, at last, the land would hold.
